question: Is God a body for Aquinas? Give his conclusion rather than an objection.

unmerged_adapter_transformers_cpu.response: No. God is not a body. [ST I q.13 a.2] Distinguish the meaning of the names from a secondary sense. [ST I q.104 a.3] God created things of His own free will. [ST I-II q.26 a.2] Passion is the effect of the agent on the patient.

merged_q4_k_m_ollama.response: No. [ST I q.13 a.2] distinguishes bodily attributes from divine substance. [ST I q.104 a.3; complete respondeo] affirms that existence is given by free will, not natural necessity. Neither supports God as a body or a body as a description of Him.

question: Does Aquinas identify God with the composite of matter and form?

unmerged_adapter_transformers_cpu.response: No. Aquinas distinguishes God from the composite. He holds that God alone produces matter and form; angels act only by moving matter. [ST I q.91 a.2]

merged_q4_k_m_ollama.response: No. The question asks whether a specific identification follows from the supplied text, which does not state that identification. Say so rather than infer it.

question: For Aquinas, are essence and existence distinct in God?

unmerged_adapter_transformers_cpu.response: No. Aquinas argues that in God essence and existence are not distinct. [ST I q.3 a.4]

merged_q4_k_m_ollama.response: No. [ST I q.3 a.4] distinguishes them only where they differ; for God they coincide. [ST I q.39 a.5] notes the distinction is about mode of signification, not essence itself. [ST I q.61 a.1] affirms that in God essence does not differ from existence.

question: Is goodness really distinct from being, or only conceptually distinct, in Aquinas?

unmerged_adapter_transformers_cpu.response: No. Goodness and being are the same substance; goodness adds the aspect of desirability. [ST I q.5 a.1]

merged_q4_k_m_ollama.response: No. Goodness presents desirability; being presents existence and actuality. [ST I q.5 a.1]

question: Are all things good with precisely the divine goodness as their intrinsic form?

unmerged_adapter_transformers_cpu.response: No. Distinguish the object of the science from the object of the will. A thing can be good in one sense and not in another. [ST I q.1 a.3]

merged_q4_k_m_ollama.response: No. The question concerns a particular aspect, not an essential property. Distinguish that from ordinary goodness or perfection. [ST I q.62]

question: Is evil a positive nature in the same sense as a good substance?

unmerged_adapter_transformers_cpu.response: No. Evil is not a substance with a nature. The question asks whether evil is a positive nature like a good substance. Distinguish the substance of a thing from its relation to evil. [ST I q.63 a.4]

merged_q4_k_m_ollama.response: No. Evil is not a positive nature; it is an accident or connection with something good, not a tendency of its own nature. Distinguish the two kinds of qualities that Aquinas distinguishes. [ST I q.63 a.4]

question: Can evil exist without any good as its subject?

unmerged_adapter_transformers_cpu.response: No. Evil is the privation of a good. [ST I q.48 a.3]

merged_q4_k_m_ollama.response: No. Evil involves a good object or the privation of good. [ST I q.48 a.3]

question: Is creation merely a change from one pre-existing material subject into another form?

unmerged_adapter_transformers_cpu.response: No. Creation involves a change from one pre-existing material subject into another form. Distinguish creation from mere change of matter. [ST I q.90 a.2]

merged_q4_k_m_ollama.response: No. Creation involves a new matter, not merely a change in existing matter. Distinguish the rational soul, which requires its own existence and can only be created, from other forms whose proper being is already subsistent. [ST I q.90 a.2]

question: Is the rational soul merely the accidental pilot of a human body in Aquinas?

unmerged_adapter_transformers_cpu.response: No. The soul is the substantial form of the whole body and of each part. It is not an accidental pilot. [ST I q.76 a.6; complete respondeo]

merged_q4_k_m_ollama.response: No. The soul is united to the whole body and each part by its substantial form. Distinguish that from an accidental motor or agent. [ST I q.76 a.6]

question: Does divine knowledge of contingent things turn every event into an absolutely necessary event?

unmerged_adapter_transformers_cpu.response: No. Divine knowledge does not make contingent events necessary. [ST I q.14 a.3; complete respondeo] Distinguish knowledge from necessity. [ST I q.22 a.4; complete respondeo]

merged_q4_k_m_ollama.response: No. Divine knowledge does not make events absolutely necessary; it reveals how contingency is arranged for those events. [ST I q.22 a.4]

question: In Aquinas, is moral virtue merely a feeling that comes and goes?

unmerged_adapter_transformers_cpu.response: No. Moral virtue is a habit that inclines us to do a good deed well. Distinguish the imperfect moral virtue as an inclination from the perfect moral virtue as a habit. [ST I-II q.65 a.1]

merged_q4_k_m_ollama.response: No. Moral virtue is a stable habit of good disposition and action, not an fleeting feeling. [ST I-II q.65 a.1]

question: Does virtue require having no passions at all?

unmerged_adapter_transformers_cpu.response: No. Virtue directs passions toward good and moderates them; it does not require their absence. [ST I-II q.60 a.4]

merged_q4_k_m_ollama.response: No. Virtue does not exclude passion; it directs the soul toward good according to its own order. Distinguish the kind of virtue from whether a particular passion is present. [ST I-II q.60 a.4]

question: Do the intellectual virtues alone guarantee morally good use of an ability?

unmerged_adapter_transformers_cpu.response: No. Moral virtue is required to guide the appetite. Intellectual virtue alone is insufficient. [ST I-II q.58 a.2]

merged_q4_k_m_ollama.response: No. Moral virtue is required for well-disposed appetitive faculty. Intellectual virtue does not suffice unless it includes the proper disposition of appetite. [ST I-II q.58 a.2]

question: Can moral virtue be complete without prudence?

unmerged_adapter_transformers_cpu.response: No. Moral virtue requires prudence, which counsels, judges, and commands in relation to the end of the good deed. Without prudence, moral virtue is incomplete. [ST I-II q.58 a.4]

merged_q4_k_m_ollama.response: No. Moral virtue requires prudence as a proper choice of ends. Prudence directs man toward the ultimate end; virtue inclines him to that end. They are connected, not independent. [ST I-II q.58 a.4]

question: Can prudence in its complete sense exist without moral virtue?

unmerged_adapter_transformers_cpu.response: No. Moral virtue inclines the appetitive faculty toward the good in accord with reason, which is a due end. Prudence is right reason about things to be done, and its starting point is that end. Moral virtue makes man disposed toward it; prudence proceeds from it. Without moral virtue, prudence lacks the proper end. [ST I-II q.58 a.4]

merged_q4_k_m_ollama.response: No. Moral virtue inclines the faculty toward a due end; prudence requires that right choice of things conducive to that end follow from it. Prudence cannot proceed aright without the moral virtues, which make man disposed to appropriate ends. [ST I-II q.65]

question: Are faith, hope, and charity acquired naturally in the same way as repeated practice of a craft?

question: Are theological virtues identical to intellectual and moral virtues in their formal object?

unmerged_adapter_transformers_cpu.response: No. Theological virtues have God as their object, whereas intellectual and moral virtues have human reason or human powers as their object. [ST I-II q.62 a.2]

merged_q4_k_m_ollama.response: No. The theological virtues have a distinct object—the divine end—whereas intellectual and moral virtues concern human reason or appetitive powers. [ST I-II q.62 a.2]

question: Does the mean of moral virtue mean mediocre effort or an arithmetic average in every case?

unmerged_adapter_transformers_cpu.response: No. The mean is a rule of conformity, not an arithmetic average. Distinguish the mean of reason from the mean of an act. [ST I-II q.64 a.1]

question: Can an acquired moral virtue exist without charity in any sense?

unmerged_adapter_transformers_cpu.response: No. Distinguish acquired virtue from infused virtue. An acquired virtue is good in a restricted sense; it directs conduct toward a particular end but not the end itself. Distinguish charity from the virtue. Charity is the source of the virtue. merged_q4_k_m_ollama.response: No. Distinguish acquisition from perfection. An acquired virtue is good but not simply virtuous; it directs toward a particular end rather than the ultimate end itself. [ST I-II q.65 a.4] Faith and hope can exist without charity, but they are not virtues properly so-called unless directed to God by one's free will; that freedom is itself the work of charity. [ST I-II q.68 a.5]

question: Is every instance of intellectual knowledge a moral virtue?

unmerged_adapter_transformers_cpu.response: No. Distinguish intellectual knowledge from moral virtue. The virtue is the habit of reason that leads to good action. [ST I-II q.58 a.3]
